Chapter 7: Friendship in Flux—Letting Go and Holding On
Friendships in your twenties can feel a bit like walking on shifting sand, don’t they? Some drift away almost without you noticing, while others surprise you by growing even deeper. Gone are the old certainties—no more school schedules or shared routines to keep you close. Now, it’s all about distance, changing priorities, and that slow, sometimes painful, realization that not every friendship is meant to last forever.
Picture this: there’s a young woman who really misses the easy closeness she used to have with her college friends. Those late-night talks, the spontaneous adventures—they feel almost like another life. These days, texts can go unanswered for days, plans get postponed, and that natural rhythm of connection? It just isn’t the same. And honestly, there’s a sting in realizing that some friendships are fading—not because of a fight, but because life’s just pulling everyone in different directions.
But then, on a random afternoon, she sits down for coffee with an old friend. At first, things are a little awkward, just catching up on work and family. But as the minutes pass, something shifts. That old comfort creeps back in. They start laughing about old misadventures, sharing their worries about the future, and admitting they feel lost more often than they’d like to say out loud. And right there, it hits her—real friendship isn’t about texting every day, but about being able to pick up wherever you left off, no matter how much time has passed.
Meanwhile, new friendships start to take root—in the workplace, around the neighborhood, even at the dog park. These connections are tentative at first, built on shared interests and those small, everyday kindnesses. And She-Devil, with her endless curiosity, is usually the one breaking the ice, pulling her person into conversations with strangers who sometimes become friends.
Letting go of old friendships is always bittersweet. There’s real grief in the loss, but there’s also a deep gratitude for what you shared. Most of the time, saying goodbye isn’t dramatic—it’s just a quiet acceptance that some people are only meant to be in your story for a chapter or two. What you might not realize is how much space opens up in your life when you stop holding on to what no longer fits.
The friendships that stick around? They’re stronger for having survived the distance and the changes. There’s a new honesty—a willingness to talk about the hard stuff: anxiety, loneliness, that nagging fear of not measuring up. These conversations become a lifeline, reminding you you’re not alone in your struggles. And over time, you start to see that friendship, like everything else that matters, is a work in progress—messy, imperfect, and absolutely worth fighting for.
